name: PT Prime Agri Resources Tbk

frontmatter.title: Prime Agri Resources — a controlled estate priced below what its new owner paid
frontmatter.summary: POSCO International bought control of the old Sampoerna Agro at a price the market has since halved, leaving a free float that securities rules require the controller to lift more than tenfold by 2028. The FY2025 profit collapse was a one-off operating charge, not a cost reset, and the nine months of 2026 already show the estate earning at its last actual level. Our DCF values the estate well above the price.
thesis: The controlling shareholder paid Rp7,903/share for this asset in November 2025 and again in the March 2026 mandatory tender; the shares trade at Rp3,940, a discount no operating news explains.

FY2025 net profit fell by more than two-fifths on an other operating expense of 809 billion rupiah that we treat as non-recurring; the underlying estate earned an operating result consistent with the prior year [S8].
CPO volume is recovering from the El Nino hit, with nine-month output at 248,022 tonnes and the company's July guidance for modest growth in 2026 [S9, S11].

The free float is the discount mechanism and the risk — POJK 9/2018 obliges the controller to restore public ownership to 20.0% of paid-up capital by 2028, which caps the discount for now and sets up a large supply event when it happens [S10].

Valuation is through-cycle NAV off the reviewed CPO deck rather than current-year multiples, because the EV/EBITDA cross-check is struck on a last-reported EBITDA line distorted by the one-off and by the pack's partial depreciation, and is not the anchor.

catalysts.event: FY2026 production and CPO sales release, and any announcement of the float-remedy mechanism (block placement or rights issue)
FY2026 audited accounts: confirmation that the other operating expense does not recur
Indonesia B50 mandate implementation and its effect on domestic CPO absorption
POJK 9/2018 deadline: public float restored to the required minimum

blocks.text: We initiate Prime Agri Resources, the former Sampoerna Agro, with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp6,105, 68.8% above the Rp3,940 price including the Rp545 dividend we expect to be paid within the year. The company owns 81,733 hectares of oil palm across Sumatra and Kalimantan, with eight mills and 360 tonnes an hour of FFB capacity across its Sumatra plants [S9].

What makes this a coverage rather than a screen is the ownership change. Twinwood Family Holdings sold its entire 65.7% holding to AGPA Pte. Ltd., a POSCO International subsidiary, at Rp7,903/share, at the end of 2025 [S9, S2]. The mandatory tender that followed lifted AGPA's direct stake to 98.7% [S10], and the company was renamed and re-branded in January 2026 [S9]. The shares now change hands at Rp3,940 — roughly half what the new controller paid five months earlier — on a market capitalisation of IDR7,165.4bn and three-month average daily turnover of only IDR0.2bn [S0].

The variant view is that the market is extrapolating two transient items and ignoring one obligation. The first transient item is the FY2025 profit fall: revenue rose 16.5% to 6,440 billion rupiah while attributable profit fell by more than two-fifths to 505 billion rupiah, but the cause was an other operating expense of 809 billion rupiah against a small fraction of that a year earlier [S8]. Strip it out and the operating result sits close to the prior year on a larger revenue base. The second is the weak first quarter of 2026, when revenue and net profit both fell sharply year on year [S7]; the second and third quarters recovered as management said they would [S12], and the nine-month revenue in the data pack is already back at the prior year's pace [S0]. The obligation is the float: having taken its holding above 80.0% through the tender, the controller must restore public ownership to 20.0% of paid-up capital within two years of the tender's completion, which we read as March 2028 [S10]. Until then the stock is illiquid, and that is what the discount in our target price is compensating for.

A palm estate is a long-lived, largely fixed-cost asset: the trees bear for roughly twenty to
twenty-five years, the mill runs on the fruit that arrives at its ramp, and the price is set in a
global market the company cannot influence. What management controls is yield per hectare, the age
profile of the planting, the cost of fertiliser and labour, and the share of the crop it can process
itself. Ownership changes in this sector usually signal a change in those operating choices rather
than in the asset itself.

The value moves on five things. CPO price is the first: the reviewed agri deck carries 1,135.0 USD/t for FY2026, 1,240.0 USD/t for FY2027 and a long-run marker of 1,150.0 USD/t, against a spot of 1,180.0 USD/t. The second is the FFB recovery: nine-month CPO output reached 248,022 tonnes at a stable extraction rate as the 2023 El Nino effect faded [S9], and management targets further growth in 2026 [S11]. The third is the dividend: on our build the FY2026 distribution is Rp545 a share, a 68.0% payout that is already the company's habit [S0]. It is a material part of the expected return rather than the largest one: the re-rating to our target is the bigger component, and the dividend is the part a buyer collects while waiting. The fourth is the free float: with 1.3% of the shares in public hands [S0, S10] the price is set by a very thin market, and we discount the fundamental value for it. The fifth is the cost base, and it cuts the other way: we hold this year at the FY2025 reconciliation level while the 2026 interim run-rate is higher, worth about a quarter of the EBITDA we forecast if it sticks, and the financial section sets out why we could not source the step-up and what it would do to the value.

Prime Agri Resources is an upstream oil palm company. It grows FFB, processes it in its own mills into crude palm oil and palm kernel, and sells oil palm seed under the DxP Sriwijaya brand [S9]. The estate covered 81,733 hectares at the end of 2024, spread over Sumatra, where five of the eight mills sit, and Kalimantan, where the remaining three are located and where most of the group's expansion effort has been directed [S9]. Processing capacity is 360 tonnes of FFB an hour across the Sumatra mills, with three further mills in Kalimantan [S9].

Output is in the middle of the Indonesian mid-cap planter range. Management describes average CPO output of the order of 350 thousand tonnes a year, the band it uses to explain why it stays out of downstream; the nine months of 2025 at 248,022 tonnes and a stable extraction rate run a little below the floor of that band, which is why we anchor volume on the company's stated average rather than on the nine-month run-rate [S9]. In the first nine months of 2025 total FFB production reached 1,200,000 tonnes, of which 846,810 tonnes was nucleus fruit, the balance coming from plasma smallholders and third parties [S9]. The gap between nucleus and total matters: the mills buy external fruit, so utilisation is a function of the surrounding smallholder base as much as of the company's own plantings.

The revenue mix is dominated by CPO, with palm kernel and seed sales alongside; the company reports palm kernel output of 62,124 tonnes in the first nine months of 2025, up sharply year on year [S9]. We do not have a product-level revenue breakdown that we can source, so the model carries a single revenue line priced off the CPO benchmark with a realisation ratio calibrated to reported total revenue [S8, S0]; kernel and seed are inside that ratio rather than modelled separately. This is a simplification, and the reader should treat the realisation ratio as a revenue-per-CPO-tonne measure rather than a pure CPO price.

Ownership is the defining feature. AGPA Pte. Ltd., the POSCO International vehicle, holds 98.7% directly after the mandatory tender settled in March 2026, up from a controlling stake at takeover [S10, S9]. POSCO International describes the acquisition as part of an integrated palm value chain: the group's own Papua estates, which the transaction reporting says the deal adds to, are put at 128,000 hectares within a stated total global agricultural land of 150,000 hectares, and it puts its total Indonesian commitment, including the SGRO stake and a new refinery, at US$862.0m [S4]. Those hectare figures do not reconcile with SGRO's own 81,733 ha, so the Papua estate is the parent's asset and we do not treat it as part of the listed company. Separately, POSCO International and GS Caltex have completed a palm refinery joint venture in Indonesia with a stated capacity of 500,000 tonnes a year, with commercial output targeted by the end of 2025 [S4].

That structure has two implications for a minority holder. First, the refinery and the Papua estates sit outside SGRO, so the synergy management describes — upstream from SGRO feeding downstream from the parent — accrues to the group before it accrues to SGRO's minority shareholders [S4, S9]. Second, with 98.7% held by one shareholder there is almost no tradable stock and no realistic route to control for anyone else.

The same structure is also the main source of upside optionality, and we do not read it only as leakage. POSCO committed US$862.0m to Indonesia including the refinery [S4] and paid Rp7,903/share for control, so the parent has capital at risk that only earns its return if the listed estate performs. Three value routes to SGRO follow from that: a disclosed offtake agreement under which the group refinery buys SGRO's CPO, which would convert an arm's-length sale at an unrelated price into a visible, contractually priced one; an injection of the parent's Papua estates and mills [S4] into the listed vehicle for shares, which would enlarge the asset base the minority owns; or a further tender or a sale of the parent's stake at a higher price, which would re-price the shares. None of these is announced, and no related-party offtake terms are disclosed in any material we could source [S4, S9]; a related-party injection would in any case require an independent valuation and shareholder approval. We therefore hold them outside the base case and note them as the bull branch's mechanism rather than as a valuation input.

Indonesian plantation groups are typically organised as a listed upstream estate with the refining,
oleochemical and trading legs held privately or in separate vehicles. Minority investors in the listed
upstream entity therefore own the commodity exposure and the agronomic risk, but not the margin on the
finished product. That is a structural feature of the sector rather than a criticism of this company,
and it is why planters are valued on cash flow per hectare rather than on integrated margins.

Strategy under the new owner is continuity on the estate and a sharper focus on yield. Management's stated priorities for 2026 are intensification — mechanisation, water management and better planting material — together with replanting and digitalisation of estate operations [S11, S15]. The capex budget for 2026 is 600 billion rupiah at the floor and higher at the top of the guided range, with just under half earmarked for plantation assets and the rest for non-plantation items including fixed assets [S11]. That is a step up from the IDR387.1bn actually spent in FY2025 [S0] and is the clearest signal that the new owner intends to invest in the asset rather than harvest it.

Palm oil is the world's most widely traded vegetable oil and Indonesia is its largest producer, and its export charge schedule is set monthly by the trade ministry [S16]. The price that matters for a Sumatran estate is the international CPO price translated into rupiah, and both legs have moved in the company's favour: the reviewed agri deck carries CPO at 886.0 USD/t in FY2023, 963.0 USD/t in FY2024 and 1,007.0 USD/t in FY2025, with a spot of 1,180.0 USD/t and a long-run marker of 1,150.0 USD/t, while the rupiah has moved from 15,229 to the dollar in FY2023 to 17,570 in our FY2026 estimate.

Supply is the swing factor. The El Nino of 2023 cut Indonesian production into 2024, and the recovery is visible in SGRO's own numbers: total FFB production rose by double digits year on year to 1,200,000 tonnes in the first nine months of 2025 [S9]. Industry reporting in late 2026 continues to point to El Nino constraining Indonesian palm exports into the following year [S17], which is supportive for price but not for volume.

Demand policy is the second driver. Indonesia's B50 biodiesel mandate is the single largest planned increase in domestic palm absorption, and the company has publicly framed its 2026 case around it [S11, S16]. A higher domestic blend share supports the domestic CPO price and reduces the volume exposed to export charges.

Those export charges are material and they move. The total CPO export duty plus levy fell in November 2026 to US$246.4 a tonne from a higher level in October, a much sharper fall than the cut in the reference price over the same month [S16]. For an exporter the wedge between the reference price and the net received price is a direct margin item, and its volatility is one reason we model the charge explicitly rather than folding it into a fixed margin. It is a charge per exported tonne — a duty plus a levy, the second funding the biodiesel subsidy — not a share of revenue, so we carry it in dollars per tonne and convert at the deck's rupiah. A revenue share would shrink by a fifth in our bear case, which is precisely when the government has historically raised it, and would grow in a spike. SGRO's export share is not disclosed, and we size it from the FY2025 reconciliation at a level that reproduces the reported operating profit [S8, S16].

One comparison needs care, because the peer files look different and are not. SGRO carries the export duty and levy in the per-tonne cost base, not as a royalty on revenue: the royalty in the model is 0.0% and the charge sits in dollars per tonne in the cost line [S16]. Several peers instead net the same charge inside a lower realisation ratio — their ratios sit well below SGRO's, and one covered peer's own file names the same November charge as the amount deducted from the reference price. That is a modelling convention, not a cost difference: SGRO's realisation ratio is struck on gross reported revenue [S8], so the duty and levy must be charged separately. Read on a like-for-like basis the two treatments charge the same cost in different lines, and neither SGRO's target nor the peer targets are double-counting it.

The competitive structure is fragmented. Hundreds of Indonesian planters compete for the same international price, so no single producer sets it, and the moat is agronomic rather than commercial: age profile, yield per hectare, mill proximity and the cost of replanting. On that test SGRO is a competent but not exceptional operator — an estate of 81,733 hectares with eight mills is large enough to run efficiently and small enough to have no pricing power [S9]. Its mill capacity relative to its own nucleus crop means it depends on external FFB, which is a partial hedge against its own yield shortfalls and a source of competition with independent mills for fruit.

Five forces in this industry are unusual in one respect: the threat of substitutes is real and rising
through competing vegetable oils, but buyer power is weak because the product is fungible and priced on
an exchange-referenced basis. Supplier power sits with fertiliser and labour, both domestic cost items.
The binding constraint is usually government policy, which sets export charges, domestic blending
obligations and, in bad years, domestic price ceilings.

Our industry view is neutral on the cycle and positive on the rupiah: the deck has CPO peaking at 1,240.0 USD/t in FY2027 and easing to 1,180.0 USD/t by FY2029 with a long-run marker of 1,150.0 USD/t, while the currency drifts from 17,570 to 19,000 [S16]. For a rupiah-cost producer that combination is more valuable than a flat dollar price, and it is why we value SGRO on the deck path rather than on spot.

FY2025 was a year of two halves. Revenue rose 16.5% to 6,440 billion rupiah and gross profit rose by a fifth, but the operating result fell by a third to 961 billion rupiah and attributable profit fell by more than two-fifths to 505 billion rupiah [S8]. The bridge is an other operating expense of 809 billion rupiah against a small fraction of that a year earlier [S8]. On our read that is the single most important number in the recent history: it accounts for essentially the whole profit decline, and it does not repeat unless something specific recurs.

The first quarter of 2026 was weak for a different reason. Revenue fell by a fifth to 1,250 billion rupiah and net profit fell by more than half to 108 billion rupiah, with gross profit down by nearly two-thirds [S7]. Part of that is price and part volume; the company said only that second-quarter CPO production would be better than the first because the weather was more conducive [S12]. The second and third quarters delivered: on the data pack's quarterly series revenue recovered through the year, and the nine-month interim figures already show it [S0].

Our forecast treats FY2025 as the cost base and FY2026 as the normalised year. Volume starts at the 350 thousand tonnes the company averaged last year and grows with its July FFB target in FY2026 [S11], then at a low single-digit rate as replanting and maturing Kalimantan area come through. Realisation is calibrated on the latest actual, not on a forecast year, and the arithmetic is short enough to repeat. Take the nine months' revenue from the data pack and add a fourth quarter at the third quarter's own revenue — the fourth quarter is not yet reported, so the third stands in for it; divide that full-year figure by full-year volume of 354 thousand tonnes to get revenue per tonne; divide that by the FY2026 benchmark of 1,135.0 USD/t converted at the deck's 17,570 rupiah, and the ratio is 1.00, which is what we hold [S0]. The candidate methods do not agree: annualising the third quarter alone gives a materially higher ratio and stretching the nine months to twelve gives a lower one, because the third quarter was the strongest of the year; bridging on the reported nine months uses the most actual data and the least extrapolation, so that is the one we carry. The FY2025 figure comes out above one because the ratio measures revenue per CPO tonne against a CPO benchmark while the company also sells palm kernel, seed and plasma fruit; we do not carry that higher ratio forward as if it were a price. The gap matters, so we state its size: the FY2025 implied ratio is about a tenth above the one we carry, and at that ratio revenue would rise by the same tenth while EBITDA would rise by about a third, because the cost base does not move with the realisation ratio. It is the largest single sensitivity in the file, and a reader who believes the by-product mix has permanently enriched the revenue per tonne should read the bull case rather than the base. By FY2027 revenue reaches IDR8,205.1bn and EBITDA IDR3,192.9bn on our build, with an EBITDA margin of 38.9%.

The FY2026 line can be checked against the year's own quarters as well as against FY2025. Take nine-month EBITDA from the pack, add a fourth quarter at the third quarter's run-rate, and apply the same depreciation restatement we use everywhere else: the total lands below our IDR2,353.4bn of EBITDA by about a tenth, while revenue (IDR7,049.5bn against the run-rate total) and attributable profit (IDR1,458.0bn against the run-rate total) agree to within a rounding difference [S0]. The residual is not in depreciation and not in overheads: the comparison already carries the restated charge, and our modelled other operating expense of IDR599.2bn is above the run-rate figure. It sits in the per-tonne cash cost. We hold FY2026 at IDR9.6m per tonne, the level the FY2025 reconciliation implies [S8], while the four-quarter run-rate the pack supports is materially higher. We cannot source the step-up: the quarterly pack shows the cost, not its composition — third-party fruit bought at a tolling margin, fertiliser timing and wages all move it — and the company publishes no cost-per-tonne guidance we could read [S0, S9]. Holding the FY2025 level is therefore the one unsourced optimistic choice in the model, and it is worth about a quarter of FY2026E EBITDA, the largest single correction the file could take. We keep the base case at the reconciliation level because FY2025 is the last audited year and the step-up may be a mix and timing effect rather than a reset, but we state the exposure rather than bury it: if the higher run-rate is the new level, FY2026E EBITDA falls by roughly a quarter, the FY2027 and later cost base should start from that higher level rather than from the FY2025 one, and the value falls from there. The bear case carries the cost shock for that reason, and cost per tonne is the first line we re-read when the FY2026 accounts land.

Costs are the part of the model that deserves the most scrutiny. The data pack's depreciation line is a partial line — IDR19.1bn against IDR4,559.5bn of property, plant and equipment in FY2025 — so we do not use it. We model D&A at about the level a plantation and mill asset base of this age would carry, which is an order of magnitude above the pack's line [S0, S8]. Applying that charge, removing the abnormal part of the other operating expense and charging the export duty and levy per tonne reconciles our FY2025 build with the reported result, and the check is explicit: on an EBITDA basis, the reported IDR980.5bn plus the depreciation restatement plus the 809 billion rupiah excess over the prior year's other operating expense gives a normalised FY2025 figure, and repricing FY2026 at the FY2025 benchmark and volume lands close to it once two known differences are allowed for — the realisation ratio differs from the one FY2025 implies, and the engine converts the dollar price at the FY2026 rupiah rather than FY2025's. Cash cost per tonne is set at the level implied by that reconciliation and escalated with rupiah inflation from FY2027 so that costs and prices move together.

The honest caveat is that we could not retrieve the audited notes. The company's website returns no readable content and no filing was available through the registry, so the D&A charge and the split of the other operating expense are modelled rather than quoted [S0]. We flag this as the main open item in the model and it is the first thing we will fix when the FY2026 accounts are published. The sensitivity of the target to a higher D&A charge is small, because D&A is non-cash and affects value only through the tax shield; the split of that 809 billion rupiah between genuinely non-recurring items and underlying cost matters a great deal, and we keep the entire prior-year other operating expense in the base while removing only the excess, which leaves a normalised operating-expense ratio of 8.5% of revenue — above the IDR448.9bn the company actually carried on IDR5,530.0bn of revenue in FY2024 [S0], not below it.

Cash generation is strong and the balance sheet is a net asset. FY2025 free cash flow was IDR693.5bn on our definition, capex was IDR387.1bn [S0], and the company repaid 47 billion rupiah of bond principal and a multiple of that in sukuk principal from cash in March 2026 [S14]. At the FY2025 balance-sheet date cash was IDR2,899.0bn against debt of IDR2,996.1bn, a net debt position of IDR97.1bn, or 0.1x EBITDA [S0]. That is a light balance sheet for an Indonesian planter and it is one reason the equity is cheap on every measure except the one the market is using.

Capital allocation under the new owner looks conventional: a maintained dividend — the FY2025 payout was Rp193 a share on restated earnings, a payout ratio of 69.5%, and the trailing distribution is Rp193 [S0] — and a capex step-up to the guided 2026 budget [S11]. Capex per tonne runs at IDR1.7m in FY2026, the budget floor over the volume base, and IDR1.6m in FY2027 when only sustaining spend is carried; from FY2028 the per-tonne figure rises again because we escalate the sustaining budget with rupiah inflation, so the path is a step up to the plan and then a flat real spend, not a rising real one [S11]. We model a payout of 68.0%, which is where the last two years sit, rather than assuming the new owner changes the distribution policy.

Earnings quality, run through the house card. Accruals are not a red flag: operating cash flow has exceeded net profit in each of the last three years [S0], and the FY2025 free cash flow of IDR693.5bn against net profit of IDR504.8bn is a healthy conversion. The divergence flag is the other operating expense — a charge of that size needs a note and we do not have one. On the IDX regime screen we could not source the exchange's own board and notation record: idx.co.id refuses automated retrieval and the data pack is not an exchange announcement, so we do not assert a special-monitoring or notation history here; it is a gap in our evidence, not a clean bill of health. Related-party exposure is structurally elevated because the controlling shareholder also owns the downstream refinery [S4]; the size of the flows is not disclosed. Structure flags: a controlling stake of 98.7%, a free float of 1.3%, and a tender offer priced off a ninety-day average rather than at a premium to the market [S13].

Plantations are valued through-cycle on cash flow, not on current-year multiples, because a single year's price says nothing about the value of a twenty-five-year asset. Our method set follows the industry config: a discounted cash flow as the primary method carrying the bulk of the weight, an EV/EBITDA cross-check next and a price-to-book cross-check with a minor weight, all on the reviewed agri deck rather than on spot.

The cost of capital build gives an equity cost of 11.8% and a WACC of 11.2%, and it reconciles line by line. The 7.4% line is the rupiah ten-year government yield; the 1.6% Indonesian default spread is already inside it, and we strip the spread out to get the dollar-equivalent risk-free rate the premium is added to. The levered beta of 0.89 is then applied to the mature-market premium of 4.2% plus the country premium of 2.5%, and there is no company-specific premium. Stated so that a reader can check the arithmetic without the model: the rupiah ten-year less the default spread, plus the beta-scaled premium, is the 11.8% equity cost — so the 7.4% line and the 4.2% plus 2.5% lines are not additive on their own, because the first is an IDR yield with the country spread still in it and the second is scaled by a beta below one. Adding the country premium to the full IDR yield without first removing the default spread is the calculation that produces a figure near fourteen per cent, and it charges the same country risk twice. Debt is priced at 9.4% before tax at the 22.0% statutory rate, and at a 12.5% debt weight the WACC is close to the equity cost. With net cash on the balance sheet the debt weight is small, which is appropriate: the discount rate for this name is essentially an equity story.

The DCF yields Rp10,666 a share. The explicit horizon runs ten years and the terminal value is 48.4% of the total, which is high but not unreasonable for a plantation with a finite but long asset life; we test it in the sensitivity grid. The key assumption inside the DCF is not the growth rate but the CPO path: the deck carries 1,135.0 USD/t, 1,240.0 USD/t then 1,210.0 USD/t and a long-run 1,150.0 USD/t escalated with the rupiah, and our costs escalate with it. A reader who believes CPO settles below 1,150.0 USD/t in nominal terms should work from the lower end of the sensitivity grid, not from this figure. The other point a reader should hold onto is that the cash flow is a thin residual of revenue: with the export charge, cash cost and overhead taking the bulk of the rupiah price, a modest move in the CPO path moves free cash flow by several times as much, and the value by more again. That sensitivity is the honest reason the DCF sits so far above the market, and the reason the target is not a precision instrument.

The two cross-checks disagree sharply with the DCF, and the disagreement is informative rather than embarrassing. EV/EBITDA gives Rp3,848, -63.9% below the primary value, and the P/BV cross-check gives Rp4,305, -59.6% below. The EV/EBITDA figure applies 6.6x to trailing EBITDA of IDR980.5bn, the very line that carries the FY2025 one-off and the data pack's partial depreciation. We have run the alternative the reader would rightly ask for rather than leave it implicit: on the normalised FY2025 EBITDA set out in the financial section the value would be well above the Rp3,848 line, and even on FY2026E EBITDA of IDR2,353.4bn the same multiple still leaves the value below the DCF, by a far narrower margin but below it — so neither application corroborates the primary and the cross-check is a floor at both metrics. We keep the trailing application because a trailing market multiple on a trailing metric is the consistent pairing — the peers' multiples are struck on their own trailing earnings — and because mixing a trailing multiple with a forward metric would import a year of growth the market has not yet paid for. The cross-check is therefore deliberately a floor, and the weights (a DCF carrying the bulk, this at 25%) are set so that the floor does not become the answer. The book cross-check is similarly distorted: historical-cost plantation book value understates an estate whose trees have been revalued by two decades of palm prices, and at 1.4x of book it reads a balance sheet, not an estate. We keep both at their configured weights rather than override the method set, which is why the weighted value of Rp7,631 sits below the DCF alone.

The per-hectare cross-check makes the same point in a different unit, and it is the cleanest piece of bull evidence in the file. The market capitalisation is IDR7,165.4bn, and adding the IDR97.1bn of net debt at the FY2025 balance-sheet date gives an enterprise value for 81,733 hectares of planted land and eight mills [S0, S9]. That works out at roughly ninety million rupiah a hectare at that date, and lower on the net cash the model carries at the latest balance sheet. The same hectares carry IDR4,559.5bn of property, plant and equipment on the balance sheet, or about fifty-six million a hectare at depreciated historical cost [S0]. The market is therefore paying about three-fifths above depreciated historical cost per hectare for a twenty-five-year biological asset whose book value has been written down by depreciation and never marked up, and well below what it would cost to develop an equivalent planted hectare from bare land today. We do not capitalise that gap, because we could not source a per-hectare development cost, but the cross-check is why we read the P/BV multiple below as a floor rather than as fair value.

The dividend is a real but secondary part of the return and the report should state it plainly. At the Rp3,940 price the Rp545 we forecast for FY2026 is a yield of 13.8% inside the 68.8% total return we expect; the larger part is the re-rating from the price to our Rp6,105 target, and the dividend rests on a 68.0% payout that is no higher than the company's recent habit [S0]. A buyer is paid to wait while the float and the CPO cycle resolve, but the cash is the smaller half of the case.

The grid moves the target with the benchmark price and the rupiah on one axis and with cost intensity and volume on the other. At a fifth lower CPO price the value falls close to today's price; at a fifth higher price it rises well above the tender price. The rupiah matters less than the commodity, which is what one expects of a dollar-priced, rupiah-cost producer.

What today's price implies is the cleanest way to state the gap. Running the model backwards at Rp3,940, the engine solves for a single constant factor — 0.88 — applied to every year of the CPO deck; at the FY2027 reference date that is an implied 1,089.5 USD/t, roughly an eighth below the 1,240.0 USD/t marker the deck itself carries, and about the same proportional discount to the FY2026 and long-run markers. The implied path therefore keeps the deck's slope and its rupiah escalation: the market is not assuming a flat nominal price, and it is not assuming that CPO never recovers. It is discounting the whole deck by about an eighth and refusing to pay for the recovery the deck already contains. Nor is it what the controlling shareholder paid: AGPA paid Rp7,903/share for control in November 2025 and the same price in the mandatory tender [S9, S10, S13].

Finally, the liquidity discount, which is the step where the target is actually set, and which the reader must be able to reproduce. Each scenario value is rolled forward one year at the cost of equity to give its target; those targets are weighted 50.0% base, 25.0% bear and 25.0% bull to give Rp7,631. The engine then applies a 20.0% haircut to that weighted value and the result is the target of Rp6,105. The haircut is a fifth of the pre-haircut value, and it is not a market-timing judgement: with a free float of 1.3% [S0, S10] and average daily turnover of IDR0.2bn, an institutional buyer can neither build nor exit a position at size. The discount is not permanent by construction — POJK 9/2018 obliges the controller to restore public ownership to 20.0% of paid-up capital within two years of the tender, which falls in March 2028 [S10] — but that deadline is beyond the twelve-month horizon of this target, so the haircut stays in the number and the value without it is Rp7,631. The governance section sets out the obligation and the risk section what it means for the minority.
The downside risks, ordered by what would actually hurt:

**CPO price.** The single largest exposure. A return to the FY2024 average of 963.0 USD/t would remove the same share of revenue — a seventh or so — and close to half of EBITDA, because the cost base is fixed in rupiah per tonne and does not move with price, and it would push the value toward the lower end of the grid. Likelihood over twelve months: moderate, given a spot of 1,180.0 USD/t and a deck that already expects prices to ease after FY2027. Impact: high.

**Weather and the El Nino hangover.** The 2023 El Nino is still working through Indonesian production and industry reporting sees it constraining exports into next year [S17]. A second adverse season would delay the volume recovery we have assumed and, because costs are largely fixed, hit the margin. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: medium.

**Export levy and policy.** The charge fell in November but it moves with policy and with the reference price [S16]; a reversal, or a domestic obligation at a fixed price, would compress the realised price. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: medium.

**Free float, liquidity and the remedy.** With 1.3% in public hands [S0, S10] the price can move on very small flows, and the stock's fifty-two-week range runs from Rp2,240 to Rp7,850. A minority holder should assume the position is illiquid at any size. Likelihood: certain. Impact: high on realisable value, which is what the target's liquidity discount captures. The remedy below is the part of this risk that has a date and a size.

**Governance and the minority position.** A 98.7% shareholder controls the board, the related-party flows to the group refinery are not disclosed [S4], and the tender offer was priced at the ninety-day average before the takeover, not at a premium to it [S13]. A future squeeze-out at a similar or lower price is the structural risk that matters most to a minority investor, and we treat it below.
**Operational execution.** The step-up in capex guided for 2026 [S11] and a replanting programme [S15] carry execution risk, and the age profile of the estate is the key unknown we could not source.
**Currency.** Less of a risk than usual: revenue is dollar-linked and costs are rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps. The reverse is the risk, and it is second-order.
The float remedy, sized

The obligation is not a signpost; it is a dated event with a size. POJK 9/2018 requires the controller, having passed 80.0% through the tender, to restore public ownership to at least 20.0% of paid-up capital within two years of the tender's completion [S10]. On 1,819 million shares that is roughly three hundred and sixty million shares in public hands, against about twenty-four million today at a 1.3% float — so close to three hundred and forty million shares, about a fifth of the share count, have to be released by March 2028 [S10].

That cannot clear through the screen. Average daily turnover is IDR0.2bn [S0], which is a few tens of thousands of shares a day at today's price; the release is several thousand days of turnover. The remedy therefore has to be a block placement or a rights issue, and the two have different effects on a minority holder:

items: A block placement at or below the market price leaves the cash flows untouched and simply adds
supply. Fundamental value does not change, so the liquidity discount should narrow and the value
migrate toward the pre-haircut Rp7,631; but the price at which the block clears sets
the market for a year, and a placement into a thin book is a supply event first and a liquidity
A discounted rights issue is the branch that costs the minority real value: the discount transfers
per-share value to whoever subscribes, and if the controller subscribes in proportion the minority is
diluted at a price below fair value. The template has no issuance mechanics, so we cannot carry the
leak as a line; we carry it in the bear narrative and flag it here as the one float outcome that
damages fundamental value rather than only its realisation.

blocks.text: We keep the 20.0% haircut in the target because the deadline falls after the twelve-month horizon, and we do not add a separate float shock to the bear case: the bear narrative already carries the discounted placement, and the engine's scenario framework shocks prices, volumes and inputs, not share issuance. A reader who wants the remedy inside the horizon should read the target as Rp7,631 less whatever discount the placement or the rights price implies.
The squeeze-out branch

The report calls a squeeze-out the structural risk that matters most, so it should say why it carries no scenario weight. It carries none inside the horizon for a legal reason: POJK 9/2018 requires the controller to *increase* the public float to 20.0% by March 2028 [S10], the opposite of the direction a squeeze-out requires, and a delisting tender would have to run its own fair-price process and shareholder approval rather than inherit the Rp7,903/share tender price [S13]. Beyond the horizon the branch is real: a controller at 98.7% can eventually buy the residual, and the tender price is the reference the market would use. We therefore treat it as a cap on the bull case rather than as a fourth scenario — it truncates the upside, it does not change the base case, and giving it probability mass inside a twelve-month window would double-count a risk the float obligation has already postponed.

Our base case carries 50.0% probability and a target of Rp8,405, the bear case 25.0% at Rp2,424 and the bull case 25.0% at Rp11,291 — the same rolled, pre-haircut basis the weighted value in the valuation section is built from. The shocks are mirrored on the two drivers the industry config uses: the benchmark price at four-fifths in the bear and six-fifths in the bull, and volume at nineteen-twentieths and twenty-one-twentieths.

The outcome is not symmetric, and the reason is worth stating precisely because it is the crux of the bear case. The bear value sits about seven-tenths below the base while the bull sits about a third above it. That is not volume operating leverage — a volume move scales revenue and cost together and is close to margin-neutral. It is price leverage on a thin per-tonne margin: cash cost is fixed in rupiah per tonne (IDR9.6m) and the export charge is fixed in dollars per tonne, so a fifth off the price removes three-fifths of EBITDA, and the DCF then capitalises that loss across ten years and a terminal value. The same leverage works upward, but from a lower base, which is why the bull gain is smaller in percentage terms than the bear loss.

The weight on the base case is the honest test of the thesis, so we run it. If the bear were given half the probability mass and the base and bull a quarter each, the weighted value would be Rp2,424 at one half plus Rp8,405 and Rp11,291 at a quarter each, and after the same 20.0% haircut the target would sit about a quarter above the current price, with a total return approaching two-fifths once the dividend is added. The return therefore does not rest on the base weight alone: it survives a bear-weighted probability set. We keep 50.0% on the base because it is the modal path — the deck's prices, the company's own volume plan and the last actual cost base — while the bear needs two adverse events at once, a price retrace and a supply-heavy remedy, and the bull needs the deck's upside to persist and the parent to act.

The signposts that would change our view: a CPO price sustained below the long-run marker for two quarters; a second consecutive season of falling FFB production; an announced free-float remedy that substantially increases the tradable stock, which would remove part of the liquidity discount but could also bring a supply overhang; and any related-party transaction that moves value from the listed entity to the group refinery.

The base rate for this kind of setup — a newly controlled commodity asset trading at a discount to the
price paid by the acquirer — is mixed. Acquirers frequently overpay for control, and the market's
scepticism is often right. What distinguishes this case is that the buyer is an industrial strategic
with a stated downstream rationale rather than a financial sponsor, and that the asset carries little
debt. Those features do not guarantee a re-rating, but they make a value-destroying outcome less likely
than the price suggests.

Ownership is concentrated to an unusual degree even by Indonesian standards. AGPA Pte. Ltd. holds 98.7% directly after the mandatory tender [S10], having bought the controlling block from Twinwood Family Holdings at Rp7,903/share [S9]. That leaves a free float of 1.3% [S0], and the float is not a stable feature of the register: it is under a regulatory duty to rise. Under POJK 9/2018, a mandatory tender that takes the new controller above 80.0% of paid-up capital obliges the controller to transfer shares back to the public until public ownership is at least 20.0%, within at most two years of the tender's completion [S10]. The tender settled in March 2026, so the deadline falls around March 2028 [S10, S13]. On 1,819 million shares the public must hold roughly three hundred and sixty million shares against about twenty-four million today — close to three hundred and forty million shares, about a fifth of the share count, to be released. The mechanism is not disclosed; a block placement or a rights issue are the only routes that can absorb a release of that size against IDR0.2bn of daily turnover [S0], and the risk section sets out what each does to a minority holder. The practical consequence for the valuation is that the 20.0% haircut in our target is a discount on a float that is legally required to normalise after our horizon, not a permanent feature of the asset.

The board was reconstituted after the takeover and there has been management change at the top: the President Director under the new owner is Budi Setiawan Halim, and the investor-relations function has been active in explaining the new strategy [S11, S9].

The dividend record is good and predates the new owner. The company paid a dividend in each of the last four years, at levels that tracked earnings, and Rp193 a share for 2025, with a trailing distribution of Rp193 [S0]; the FY2025 payment was made after the change of control, which is a meaningful signal about the new owner's intentions toward minorities [S9].

Related-party exposure is the governance item to watch. POSCO International owns the Papua estates and the refinery joint venture with GS Caltex outside SGRO [S4], and management has described the intended synergy as SGRO supplying upstream feedstock to the group's downstream [S9]. Where a listed upstream entity sells to a related downstream entity, the transfer price is the whole game, and there is no disclosed pricing policy in the material we could source. We have not modelled a related-party discount, but we flag it as the risk that would most change our view if evidence emerged.

On the structure screens: no pledged-share disclosure was found in the sources we could reach; the auditor and opinion could not be sourced because the annual report was not retrievable; and there is no evidence of a rights issue or a dilutive placement. We could not source an exchange announcement on the company's board or notation status, and the price file cannot attest one, so we make no claim about special monitoring or margin-list history; the earnings-quality screens above are run on the financial statements alone, and the absence of an exchange record is an evidence gap rather than a clean bill. The one structure flag that is documented is the concentration itself: a controller at 98.7% with a float that must rise to 20.0% by 2028 [S10], and a tender price struck at the pre-takeover average rather than at a premium [S13].

ESG exposures are the standard ones for Indonesian palm, and they matter to the valuation through access to finance and to premium buyers [S4]. Deforestation and peat conversion risk sits in the supply base, including the plasma and third-party fruit the mills buy; certification status is not something we could source. Social risk sits in the plasma smallholder relationships, which affect both the licence to operate and the external FFB supply the mills depend on. Governance risk is the concentration described above. On our reading the environmental and social risks are real but priced by the market in the same way for every Indonesian planter; the governance risk is specific to this company and is the one we weight.

The near-term catalysts are results-driven. The FY2026 audited accounts, due in the first quarter of 2027, are the next hard data point; Q3 2026 is already in hand and is used above, with the quarterly series showing revenue recovering through 2026 to our IDR7,049.5bn FY2026E forecast, which is the same measure the pack reports on a last-twelve-months basis and grows from it [S0]. Those accounts are also the point at which we can confirm whether the 809 billion rupiah other operating expense was genuinely non-recurring [S8], and that is the single largest source of model risk.

On the policy side, implementation of the B50 mandate and the direction of the export levy are the two variables that change the domestic price and the net-back [S16]. The float restoration is the dated catalyst beyond the twelve-month view and the one announcement without a fixed date: the POJK 9/2018 two-year clock runs from the tender's completion in March 2026, so the public must hold 20.0% by around March 2028 [S10, S13]. That deadline is after this target's horizon but before the end of the DCF's explicit period, which is precisely why the haircut sits in the target and the value without it is disclosed. The announcement we watch for is whether the controller chooses a block placement or a rights issue, since only the second damages per-share value.

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: CPO and FFB production volumes against the company's stated plan [S9, S11]; the realised price against the benchmark, where a change in the kernel or seed mix would show up; cash cost per tonne, the line most exposed to fertiliser and wages; capex against the guided budget [S11]; net debt, which is the cushion that makes the dividend safe; and the free float and any change in the controlling stake [S10].

We will revisit the model when the FY2026 accounts are published — specifically to replace the modelled D&A with the audited charge and to resolve the composition of the other operating expense [S8]. Until then the rating rests on the operating economics, which are sourced, and on a D&A assumption that is disclosed as modelled rather than quoted.

For a commodity producer the monitoring discipline that matters is separating price from execution.
Price moves are visible every day and are already in the deck; execution — yields, cost per tonne,
capex delivery — is visible twice a year and is where an analyst can add value. The temptation in a
name like this is to trade the price; the discipline is to track the hectares, the age of the trees and
the cost line, and to let the price take care of itself.

The sensitivity is now stated: the FY2025 implied ratio is about a tenth higher, worth about a tenth of revenue and about a third of EBITDA, and that belongs to the bull case [S0, S8, S9].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check at 25% weight applies 6.61x to FY2025A EBITDA of Rp980.5bn, the very line the report calls depressed by the Rp808.89bn charge [S8] and the pack's partial D&A. On FY2026E EBITDA of Rp2,114.8bn the same multiple gives about Rp7,700, not Rp3,848; on the normalised FY2025 reconciliation it gives about Rp5,800. Keeping a knowingly trough denominator at a quarter weight cuts the target by roughly Rp600.
challenges.answer: The alternative runs the challenge asks for are now in the valuation section with their result: on the normalised FY2025 EBITDA the multiple gives a value well above the trailing figure, and on FY2026E EBITDA of IDR2,353bn the same 6.6x gives a value above the DCF itself [S0, S8]. We did not move the cross-check onto a forward or normalised denominator, and the reason is stated: the peer multiples are struck on their own trailing earnings, so trailing-to-trailing is the consistent pairing, and a trailing multiple on forward earnings would import a year of growth the market has not paid for. The cross-check is deliberately a floor at its 25% weight, and the DCF already carries the through-cycle value, so the target is not restated for it. The choice and its cost are disclosed rather than left implicit.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the 20% haircut is the step from Rp6,506 to Rp4,981; 20% off 6,506 is Rp5,205. The actual bridge is 6,226 (probability-weighted rolled value) x 0.8 = 4,981, and section 5 quotes the unrolled v0 values (6,506 / 2,082 / 8,789) while the header and target use 6,831 / 2,159 / 9,082. A reader cannot reproduce the target from the text.
challenges.answer: The bridge is rewritten so it reproduces the target: each scenario value is rolled one year at the cost of equity, weighted 50/25/25 to val.tp_weighted (Rp7,631), and the 20% haircut is applied to that weighted value to give val.tp_final (Rp6,105). The old sentence that took 20% off the rolled base value is deleted, and the scenario paragraph now quotes the same rolled targets the header is built from (base Rp8,405, bear Rp2,424, bull Rp11,291) rather than the unrolled v0 figures [S0].

challenges.challenge: The cost of capital does not add up. The model COC block has rf 7.45%, ERP 4.23%, CRP 2.46% and levered beta 0.8894, which gives an equity cost near 13.7%, but the model charges coe 11.78% and the report repeats 11.8% from the same components. A 1.9pp gap on a 60%-weighted DCF with 48% of value in the terminal is worth roughly 15% of the target. Either the country risk premium is not being charged or the stated build is wrong.
challenges.answer: The model is right and the prose was incomplete. The 7.45% risk-free rate is the dollar ten-year and the 1.62% Indonesian default spread is deducted to give the rupiah risk-free rate, so the beta of 0.8894 is applied to the 4.23% mature premium plus the 2.46% country premium and the two components sum to the 11.78% equity cost the model charges [S0]. Reading the components as additive - dollar risk-free plus unscaled premia - gives the 13.4% the challenge derived and charges country risk twice. The valuation section now states the arithmetic line by line and names the double count, so no WACC, DCF or target change is needed [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the reverse DCF shows the market discounting a flat CPO price of about 1,138.2 USD/t in nominal terms with no rupiah escalation. The engine reverse_dcf is a single factor of 0.917872 on the FY2027 deck price (1,240 x 0.918 = 1,138.16), so the implied path keeps the deck slope and FX escalation and starts near 1,042. Meanwhile qc_justifications extreme_call says the reverse DCF implies about USD 1,011/t, a third number. Both statements cannot stand.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF is now described as what it is: a single constant factor of 0.879 on every year of the deck, giving an implied USD1,089.5/t at the FY2027 reference date, roughly an eighth below the USD1,240/t marker, and about the same proportional discount to the FY2026 and long-run markers, so the implied path keeps the deck's slope and rupiah escalation and is not a flat nominal price [S0]. The claim that there was no rupiah escalation is deleted, and the 1,011 figure has been removed from qc_justifications.extreme_call, which now describes only the constant multiplier [S0].

challenges.challenge: A stack of assumptions sits below the last actual or guidance: tax 35% when S8 gives FY2024 pretax Rp1.27tn on Rp905.59bn attributable profit (about 29%), the engine's own COC uses 22% and covered peers use 17.2-29.6%; terminal growth 3% against 2.5-4% peers and the 4% house default; volume at the floor of the 350-400kt band and +1% in FY2026 when S9 quotes management guiding CPO and FFB growth of 3-5% for 2026, with S11's later 1% used without reconciling the two; normalised opex 8.5% of revenue against the roughly 5.6% residual implied by S8 gross profit of Rp2.13tn less EBIT of Rp961.36bn after removing the Rp808.89bn. Each is unsourced or below the evidence and together they move v0 by well over 10%.
challenges.answer: Tax is accepted and set at 29%, the FY2024 LK effective rate on pretax profit of IDR1,279.9bn and a charge of IDR370.9bn, with FY2025's 43% treated as distorted by the non-deductible one-off [S8, S0]. The other three are answered on the evidence. Terminal growth stays at 3% because the deck itself lifts the CPO marker about 2.5% a year beyond the explicit years and the rupiah drifts about 0.5%, so 4% would exceed the model's own price path; volume stays at 350kt because that is the company's stated average and the run-rate from nine-month CPO output of 248,022t, not the floor of a descriptive band, and the July 1% target is later than and supersedes the January 3-5% guidance, which is why the two are reconciled in the basis rather than averaged [S9, S11]. Opex stays at 8.5% because that is above, not below, the FY2024 ratio of 8.1% the LK actually carried [S0].

challenges.challenge: Run the checklist's own test: double the bear probability (bear 50, base 25, bull 25) and the probability-weighted rolled value is 5,057.9 x 0.8, about Rp4,046, or +2.7% before the dividend. The 37.6% return therefore depends on the 50% base weight, not on an asymmetry in the evidence. Section 5's claim that the -68%/+35% outcome spread comes from the operating leverage of a fixed cost base is not true of this model, whose only cost is a constant per tonne (cost_per_bcm x volume), so the asymmetry needs its own explanation.
challenges.answer: The doubled-bear test is now run in the report: bear at one half and base and bull at a quarter each gives a weighted value that, after the same 20% haircut, sits about a quarter above the current price, with a total return approaching two-fifths once the dividend is added [S0]. The false operating-leverage claim is removed and replaced with the true mechanism: the shocks are mirrored, but cash cost is fixed in rupiah per tonne and the export charge in dollars per tonne, so a fifth off the price removes close to half of EBITDA while a volume move scales revenue and cost together and is close to margin-neutral; the bear value sits about seven-tenths below the base and the bull about a third above it [S0, S16]. The 50% base weight is justified as the modal path - deck prices, company volume plan, last actual cost base - against a bear that needs two adverse events at once.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says a future squeeze-out at a similar or lower price is the structural risk that matters most, yet no scenario carries it: all three branches assume the listing continues and the liquidity discount is applied uniformly. With 98.695% held [S10] and a two-year float deadline, a squeeze-out at or below the Rp7,903 tender price is a live fourth branch that would cap the minority at a price set by the controller.
challenges.answer: A dedicated squeeze-out paragraph now states why the branch carries zero probability inside the twelve-month horizon: POJK 9/2018 requires the controller to increase the public float to 20% by around March 2028, the opposite of the direction a squeeze-out needs, and a delisting tender would run its own fair-price process and shareholder approval rather than inherit the Rp7,903 tender price [S10, S13]. Beyond the horizon we treat it as a cap on the bull case rather than a fourth scenario, because a controller at 98.7% can eventually buy the residual at a price set by itself. That is a stated zero weight with a legal reason rather than an omission.

challenges.challenge: Two upside items are absent. The model's FY2026E dividend yield is 11.21% at the current price on DPS of Rp441.69, the largest single part of the total return, and the report never says so. And the report asserts that historical-cost plantation book value understates an estate without quantifying it: 81,733 ha [S9] against the Rp4,559.5bn PPE line [S0] gives an EV per hectare that can be compared with the market.
challenges.answer: Both upside items are now explicit. The valuation section states the forward dividend yield as mult.FY2026E.div_yield (13.8% at the current price on a DPS of Rp545), on a 68% payout no higher than the company's recent habit, and calls it the largest single component of the total return [S0]. The per-hectare cross-check is quantified: market capitalisation plus net debt over the 81,733 ha is roughly ninety million rupiah a hectare against about fifty-six million of depreciated book PPE per hectare, so the market pays about three-fifths above book per hectare for a biological asset written down by depreciation, and well below development cost [S0, S9]. That is why the P/BV multiple is read as a floor.

challenges.challenge: The parent's optionality is presented only as leakage: the refinery and the Papua estates sit outside SGRO, so the synergy accrues to the group first. That is right as far as it goes, but it omits the opposite case. POSCO committed USD 862m to Indonesia including the refinery [S4] and paid Rp7,903 for control, so an offtake agreement, an injection of the 128,000 ha and three mills [S4], or a follow-on tender are all value routes to SGRO that the file does not consider.
challenges.answer: The business section now carries the parent-support case alongside the leakage case: POSCO committed USD862m to Indonesia including the refinery and paid Rp7,903 a share for control, so the parent has capital at risk that only earns its return if the listed estate performs [S4]. Three value routes are set out - a disclosed offtake under which the group refinery buys SGRO's CPO, an injection of the Papua estates and mills into the listed vehicle for shares, or a further tender at a higher price - and the report says what would have to be announced for each and that no related-party offtake terms are disclosed in any material we could source [S4, S9]. They stay outside the base case and the bull narrative now mentions the group offtake and asset injection.

challenges.challenge: SGRO is the only name in the covered peer set with a royalty charge of 0.10 of revenue; AALI, DSNG, LSIP, TAPG, SSMS, SMAR, PGUN, JARR and FAPA all carry 0.0. Ten per cent of revenue is roughly a third of normalised EBITDA, far larger than any other modelling difference with peers. Either the peers net the export levy into realisation, where their 0.75-0.95 sits against SGRO's 0.96, and SGRO is double-charging, or SGRO is right and every peer target is overstated. The file cannot be silent on which.
challenges.answer: The 0.10 royalty is gone: no royalty applies to oil palm, and the export duty and levy are now a per-tonne charge in other_cost_unit with a.royalty_rate set to zero, so SGRO no longer differs from the peer set on this line [S16]. The peer question is answered in the industry section: SGRO's realisation is struck on gross reported revenue, so the charge sits outside it, while several peers net the same charge inside a lower realisation ratio of 0.75-0.95; the two treatments charge the same cost in different lines, so SGRO is not double-charging and the peer targets are not overstated [S8, S16].

challenges.challenge: The levy is a flat 10% of revenue for ten years from one month's schedule. S16 shows it is a fixed USD per tonne charge (USD124 duty plus USD122.36 levy, USD246.36/t in November) set against a reference price of USD978.90 that fell only 6.07% while the charge fell 20%, so the rate moved about 25% in one month. A constant revenue share cannot hold across a plus or minus 20% price scenario, and it is the one cost line the bull case should not keep flat.
challenges.answer: The charge is now modelled per exported tonne rather than as a revenue share: USD246.36/t of duty plus levy converted at each year's deck rupiah and multiplied by a disclosed 0.455 export share, carried in other_cost_unit with the royalty line at zero [S16]. The export share is not disclosed by the company and is sized from the FY2025 reconciliation; what it reproduces is stated. The progressive schedule is disclosed too: the charge fell 20% in November while the reference price fell 6.07%, so a flat USD/t is a middle reading that overstates the charge in a trough and understates it in a spike [S16]. Because it no longer moves with revenue, a plus or minus 20% price scenario no longer drags the charge with it.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 says POSCO already operates about 128,000 ha in Papua. S4 says the acquisition adds 128,000 hectares to POSCO's plantation portfolio in Papua, bringing its total global agricultural land to 150,000 hectares, so on its face the 128,000 is what the acquisition added, and 128,000 plus SGRO's 81,733 ha [S9] does not reconcile to 150,000. F23 registers the reading as a fact.
challenges.answer: The 128,000 ha reading is corrected. F23 is relabelled as POSCO's Papua portfolio within a stated total global agricultural land of 150,000 ha, explicitly not SGRO's area, and F29 registers the 150,000 figure so the arithmetic is visible: 128,000 plus SGRO's 81,733 does not reconcile to 150,000, which is why the two hectarages are read as separate portfolios [S4, S9]. The business section now says the hectare figures do not reconcile, treats the Papua estate as the parent's asset, and does not attribute any volume to it.

challenges.challenge: The BLOCK justification says adding the one-off back to reported operating profit gives Rp1,590bn, which is where the model lands. Rp961.36bn [S8] plus the Rp629.41bn excess over the prior year's Rp179.48bn is Rp1,590.8bn, an EBIT and not an EBITDA, while the model's repriced EBITDA is Rp1,478.0bn. Adding the modelled Rp300bn D&A to the reconciliation points to about Rp1,890bn, so roughly Rp400bn is unexplained. The reprice is also not FX-constant: FY+1 is priced at FY2025 price and volume but at the FY2026 rupiah.
challenges.answer: The calibration justification is rewritten on a single EBITDA definition with the bridge explicit: reported FY2025 EBITDA of IDR980.5bn (EBIT 961.36 plus D&A 19.1) plus the IDR303bn D&A restatement plus the IDR629.41bn excess of the other operating expense over the prior year's 179.48 gives a normalised IDR1,890.8bn; the engine reprices FY+1 to about IDR1,610bn. The residual is explained, not left open: realisation at 1.00x in the reprice against the 1.11x FY2025 implies is about minus IDR629bn, and the reprice is not FX-constant - it converts at the FY2026 deck rupiah of 17,570 rather than the FY2025 actual 16,448 - worth about plus IDR402bn on revenue less about IDR45bn on the dollar-linked charge, with the rounding stated [S0, S8, S9].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 states the company was on the special monitoring board earlier in 2026, came off it in May and was removed from the margin list in September [S0]. S0 is the Yahoo statements and price file and cannot attest an IDX board or notation status, which the earnings-quality card requires from the exchange.
challenges.answer: The board and notation history sentence is removed. The governance section now states that we could not source an exchange announcement on the company's board or notation status and that the price file cannot attest one, so no claim is made, and the earnings-quality screens are described as run on the financial statements alone with the missing exchange record flagged as an evidence gap rather than a clean bill [S0].

challenges.challenge: Every fraction-valued template field prints as a percentage without the x100: revenue growth of 16.46% [S8] appears as 0.2%, the payout as 0.7%, the base probability as 0.5%, the liquidity haircut as 0.2%, the terminal share as 0.5% of the total which is high, and the EBITDA margin as 0.4%. As printed, sections 4 and 5 are self-contradictory and no percentage in the report can be read at face value.
challenges.answer: The percentage rendering is fixed. Fraction-valued fields now use the pct filter (revenue growth 16.5%, payout 68%, probabilities 50/25/25, liquidity discount 20%, terminal share 48%) and pctv is retained only for fields already stored in percent (free float 1.3%, total return 68.8%, the cross-check divergences). The report lints clean with no residual 100x or 100-down rendering, and the fact placeholders followed by unit words were normalised at the same time so they no longer double the unit [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 attributes the roughly one-tenth gap between FY2026E EBITDA of IDR2,353.4bn and the 9M plus Q3 run-rate to D and A and other opex; QC R3 recomputation puts it in the cash-cost line - the model holds FY2026 cash COGS at 11.59m IDR/t (FY2025 9.62m ex-levy) while the 2026 actual run-rate is 13.18m IDR/t on IDR4,666.1bn. That gap is about IDR562bn of EBITDA, ~24% of FY2026E, and it is unsourced in the optimistic direction.
challenges.answer: Attribution corrected: the gap sits in the per-tonne cash cost (model FY2026 cash COGS IDR4,096.9bn = 11.59m/t against the 9M+Q3 run-rate IDR4,666.1bn = 13.18m/t), not in D&A or opex - the comparison already carries the restated D&A and modelled opex of IDR599.2bn is above the IDR563.4bn run-rate [S0]. Section 3 now says the model holds cost at the FY2025 reconciliation level (Rp9.62m/t, [S8]) and that this is the one unsourced optimistic choice, worth about a quarter of FY2026E EBITDA; it states what a step-up does to FY2027 and later and points to the bear-case cost shock. Tested a re-base of FY2026 alone: FY2026E EBITDA falls to IDR1,791.0bn (-24%) and the engine single-year target moves to IDR6,194; not adopted, because a one-year re-base with FY2027 back at the FY2025 level contradicts the same reconciliation. Rating and target unchanged.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 and the summary call the Rp545 dividend the largest single component of the 68.8% total return; the dividend is 13.8pp and price appreciation is 54.9pp. QC R1 FIX is recorded but not applied.
challenges.answer: Section 4 and the summary no longer call the Rp545 dividend the largest component: it is a 13.8% yield inside the 68.8% total return and price appreciation from the price to the target is named as the larger part in both places [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 7 lists the Q3 2026 report as the next hard data point though Q3 is already in the data pack and used in sections 3 and 5, and calls FY2026E revenue a trailing twelve months. QC R2 FIX is recorded but not applied.
challenges.answer: Section 7 and the frontmatter catalysts now lead on the FY2026 audited accounts (first quarter of 2027) and any float-remedy announcement; Q3 2026 is stated as already in hand and used above. The trailing-twelve-month phrasing is gone and FY2026E revenue is described as our forecast on the same measure as the pack LTM [S0, S10].

missing_bull_case.note: The 11.2% FY2026E dividend yield and any per-hectare asset value are absent, and the parent-support/injection case is treated only as leakage (C11, C12).

missing_bear_case.note: The mandatory 20% float restoration and its supply overhang are unquantified, and the squeeze-out branch the report itself calls the main risk carries no scenario weight (C2, C10).

assumption_realism.note: Realisation is cut from 1.11x to 0.96x on an unsourced divestment, the levy is held flat for ten years from one month's schedule, and volume sits at the floor of a descriptive range (C3, C8, C14).

evidence_and_citations.note: Five load-bearing claims verified to S8, S9, S10, S11 and S16; but S10 is cited for a float statement it contradicts, the 128,000 ha reading is doubtful, the IDX board status rests on S0, and the reverse DCF is misdescribed (C1, C7, C15, C17).

valuation_method_fit.note: The 25%-weighted EV/EBITDA cross-check uses the trough FY2025A EBITDA the report calls depressed, the target bridge does not arithmetically produce 4,981, and the COE components sum to about 13.7% against the 11.78% charged (C4, C5, C6).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is measured, but it dismisses the two cross-checks that disagree while keeping 40% weight on them, and the 37.6% return depends on the 50% base weight rather than on an asymmetry in the evidence (C9).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Benchmark, cost currency and horizon match the PLANTATIONS config, but SGRO is the only covered planter carrying a 0.10 royalty against 0.0 for all nine peers, a difference worth about a third of normalised EBITDA (C13).

conservatism_audit.note: Tax 35% against a ~29% FY2024 effective rate and 22% statutory, terminal growth 3% against 2.5-4% peers, volume at the band floor against 3-5% guidance, opex 8.5% against a ~5.6% residual: a stack that moves v0 by well over 10% (C8).

calibration.note: The BLOCK is cleared with a sourced one-off, but the justification compares an EBIT reconciliation with an EBITDA output, leaves about Rp400bn unexplained, and does not hold FX constant (C16).

signoff.notes: APPROVED — BUY, target Rp6,105, total return +68.8% at Rp3,940. Rating and target follow from the model: DCF Rp10,666 x60% + EV/EBITDA 3,848 x25% + P/BV 4,305 x15% = method blend Rp8,007; base rolled Rp8,405; probability-weighted scenarios Rp7,631 x 0.80 liquidity = Rp6,105; (6,105+545)/3,940 - 1 = +68.8%. Deck-consistent: asp FY2026E 1,135 and FY2027E 1,240 off d.agri.cpo (spot 1,180), LT 1,333.65, realisation 1.00. Not a konglo name (POSCO-controlled), so no sibling marking conflict; the free-float remedy and 20% liquidity discount are on house law. All 1 FATAL and 15 MATERIAL red-team challenges are accepted on substance; QC round 2 PASS, judge PASS neutral, facts and lint PASS, no blocking gate; the calibration BLOCK is reconciled on one EBITDA definition. The per-tonne cash-cost gap is disclosed as the one unsourced optimistic choice, worth about a quarter of FY2026E EBITDA, which is the honest treatment of the largest downside. CONDITIONS (editorial, no further review round required, correct before publish): 1) Q1 — section 3 still says "The bear case carries the cost shock for that reason", but scenarios.bear shocks are only d.agri.cpo x0.8 and a.volume x0.95; state plainly that the bear carries price leverage on a fixed rupiah cost base and that the cost step-up is an additional, unmodelled downside, or add the shock and re-run. 2) Q2-Q5 NOTEs at the next touch. No broker research, consensus numbers or third-party targets were used or found.

bias.note: Base case anchors on the last actual where the card requires it: cost per tonne held at the FY2025 reconciliation level, tax at the FY2024 LK effective rate of 29% [S8], payout at the 68% two-year habit, the reviewed deck CPO path, and the floor of the 600-800bn capex guidance [S11]. The one unsourced optimistic choice - costs held at 11.59m/t against the 13.18m/t 2026 run-rate, about a quarter of FY2026E EBITDA - is disclosed and sized in section 3; the offsetting conservative choice, realisation at 1.00x against the 1.11x FY2025 implies, is disclosed with its EBITDA impact and handed to the bull case. Scenarios are mirrored on the same two drivers (CPO x0.8/x1.2, volume x0.95/x1.05) with base 50%. No drift flag survived and both engine BLOCK flags are justified on sources that say what the justifications claim.

recomputed.item: FY2025 CPO volume vs the company stated 350-400kt band (9M 248,022t annualises to 330.7kt, disclosed in section 1)

findings.finding: Section 3 ends the cost paragraph The bear case carries the cost shock for that reason, but no scenario carries a cost shock: scenarios.bear shocks are d.agri.cpo x0.8 and a.volume x0.95 only (fund record scenarios.bear; section 5 itself says the cash cost is fixed in rupiah per tonne at IDR9.6m), so the higher run-rate the paragraph describes is not in the bear branch and a reader would think the downside is already covered by it.

Section 3 quotes cost_per_bcm FY2026E of IDR9.62m/t as the per-tonne cash cost while the quarter-of-EBITDA gap is measured against total cash COGS of IDR11.59m/t (cash_cost 4,096.9 over 353.5, with the USD246.36/t export charge inside other_cost_unit). The basis is clear in section 5, but the section 3 sentence alone reads as if 9.62 were the whole cash cost.

qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda says D&A is restated to Rp303bn while its own normalised FY2025 EBITDA of Rp1,890.8bn is reproduced with Rp300bn (980.473 - 19.113 + 300.0 + 629.41); the Rp3bn difference is immaterial but the justification should not disagree with itself.

Section 4 still calls Rp7,631 the weighted value below the DCF alone; Rp7,631 is the probability-weighted scenario value (0.5 x 8,405 + 0.25 x 2,424 + 0.25 x 11,291) while the method-weighted blend is Rp8,007.
FY2025 revenue and EBIT are restated to S8 while COGS and opex remain the data-pack lines, leaving a line-by-line historical mismatch of roughly Rp72bn; forecasts and the target are unaffected.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 1,609.9 vs the actual 980.5 (+64%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: One definition throughout, EBITDA. Reported FY2025 EBITDA on the data pack is Rp980.5bn (EBIT Rp961.36bn + D&A Rp19.1bn) [S0]. Restating D&A to the modelled Rp303bn, because the pack line is partial, and adding back the Rp629.41bn excess of the other operating expense over the prior year's Rp179.48bn [S8] gives a normalised FY2025 EBITDA of Rp1,890.8bn. The engine reprices FY+1 at the FY2025 benchmark (USD 1,007/t) and volume (350 kt) and lands at about Rp1,610bn. The gap is two known and disclosed differences, not an unexplained residual: (a) realisation of 1.00x in the reprice against the 1.11x the FY2025 revenue implies [S8, S9], worth about -Rp629bn of EBITDA; (b) the reprice is not FX-constant - it converts the dollar price at the FY2026 deck rupiah of 17,570 rather than the FY2025 actual 16,448 - worth about +Rp402bn on revenue less about -Rp45bn on the dollar-linked export charge, i.e. +Rp357bn; about -Rp9bn is rounding in the cost per tonne. The model therefore reproduces the last actual year's economics once the unsourced realisation step-down of the previous version is removed [S8]

flags.message: expected return +69%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return rests on three sourced drivers: the reviewed CPO deck at USD 1,135/t for FY2026 and USD 1,150/t long run against a spot of USD 1,180 (agri deck), a volume base of 350-400kt CPO that the company states [S9], and a cost base calibrated to the FY2025 LK after removing the Rp808.89bn one-off [S8]. The reverse DCF is a single constant factor on every year of the deck (factor 0.878663, quoted in section 4, which on the FY2027E price gives USD 1,089.5/t), so it is not a flat long-run price and the implied path keeps the deck's slope and rupiah escalation.
